subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Assalaamu alaykum, and welcome to Unit 3. In this unit you will study two of the biggest ideas in all of science: forces and energy. A force is a push or a pull. Energy is the thing that lets change happen. Together, these two ideas explain almost everything that moves, falls, floats, warms up, lights up or comes to a stop around you, from the camel that kneels down at your homestead to the Moon that hangs over the Indian Ocean at night.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Describe changes in energy that are a result of an event or process.
Know that energy tends to dissipate and in doing so it becomes less useful.
Describe gravity as a force of attraction between any two objects and describe how the size of the force is related to the masses of the objects.
Understand that there is no air resistance to oppose movement in a vacuum.
Describe a vacuum as a space devoid of matter.
Know that gravity is the force that holds components of the Solar System in orbit around the Sun.
Describe tidal forces on Earth as a consequence of the gravitational attraction between the Earth, Moon and Sun.
Use symbols and formulae to represent scientific ideas.

outcomes: Describe gravity as a non-contact force of attraction that exists around every object that has mass, and explain that it acts towards the centre of a planet or star.
Explain why your weight changes on the Moon and on other planets while your mass stays the same.
Describe the Solar System: the Sun at the centre, the eight planets and their orbits, and how a scientific model helps us picture what we cannot see directly.
Explain movement in space: why planets orbit the Sun, why the Earth spinning on its axis gives us day and night, and why there is no air resistance in the vacuum of space.
Explain the tides as the daily rise and fall of the ocean caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon, and describe spring tides and neap tides.
Identify the main forms of energy (kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic, chemical, thermal, light, sound and electrical) and give an everyday example of each.
Describe energy transfers, using the idea that energy is stored, then transferred from one store to another, and that some energy is always dissipated (wasted).
Apply the principle that energy is never created or destroyed, only transferred from one store to another.
Describe what a person on the beach at Mombasa would see over a period of about twelve hours as the tide comes in and goes out. What is pulling the water?
List the energy transfers that happen from the moment charcoal is lit to the moment a pot of rice is fully cooked. Which energy is useful and which is wasted?

concepts.title: Gravity: The Great Invisible Pull
concepts.explanation:
Gravity is a force of attraction that exists around every single object that has mass. That includes the Earth, the Sun, the Moon, a mountain, a camel, a grain of sand, and even you. The larger the mass of an object, the stronger the gravity around it. The Earth has an enormous mass, so its gravity is strong enough to hold everything, and everyone, firmly on its surface. Your own body has mass too, so there is a tiny amount of gravity around you as well, but it is far too weak for you to notice.

A very important idea is the direction in which gravity pulls. Earth's gravity always pulls objects towards the centre of the Earth. When you drop a stone, it does not fall sideways or upward; it falls straight down, towards the ground, because the centre of the Earth is directly beneath your feet. This is true everywhere on the planet. A child in Nairobi, a fisherman in Berbera, and a farmer in the Rift Valley all feel gravity pulling them 'down', and 'down' for each of them means towards the same centre of the Earth. This is why people on the other side of the round Earth do not fall off: for them, 'down' also points to the centre, which to us would look like 'up'.

Gravity is what gives objects their weight, and it is what causes objects to fall. When there is nothing holding an object up, gravity pulls it and it falls, faster and faster, until it hits the ground or something stops it. A date falling from a palm, rain falling from a cloud, and water pouring from a jerrican are all examples of gravity at work. Gravity also reaches far out into space. The Sun's gravity is so strong that it holds the entire Earth in its orbit, even though the Earth is about one hundred and fifty million kilometres away. The Earth's gravity holds the Moon. Gravity, then, is not just about things falling near the ground; it is the invisible thread that ties the whole Solar System together.
concepts.example: Did You Know? If you could drop a hammer and a feather at the same moment on the Moon, where there is no air at all, they would hit the ground together. An astronaut named David Scott actually did this on the Moon in 1971, and it worked exactly as the science predicts. On Earth the feather drifts down slowly only because of air resistance, not because gravity treats it differently.

concepts.title: Mass and Weight: A Difference That Really Matters
concepts.explanation:
This is one of the most important ideas in the whole unit, and also one that many people get wrong, so read it slowly. Mass and weight are not the same thing, even though in everyday talk people often use the words as if they were.

Mass is the quantity of matter in an object: how much 'stuff' it is made of. Mass is measured in kilograms (kg). A very important fact about mass is that it never changes when you move the object from place to place. A 25 kg sack of rice has a mass of 25 kg in your home, at the top of a mountain, on the Moon, or floating far out in space. Nothing about the amount of matter in the sack has changed; therefore its mass has not changed.

Weight is different. Weight is the force of gravity acting on the mass of an object. Because weight is a force, it is measured in newtons (N), not in kilograms. And here is the key point: weight depends on gravity. If you take the object somewhere with weaker gravity, such as the Moon, the object still has the same mass, but gravity pulls on it more gently, so its weight is less. The object would feel lighter and would be easier to lift, even though it contains exactly the same amount of matter.
concepts.example: Here is a way to hold the difference in your mind. Imagine your favourite goat. Its mass is the amount of goat there is, the meat and bone and hair, and that never changes no matter where the goat stands. Its weight is how hard the Earth pulls that goat downward, which is what you would feel if you tried to lift it. On the Moon the goat would be exactly the same goat, same mass, but it would be far easier to lift because the Moon's gravity is weaker. So: mass is what you are made of; weight is how hard gravity pulls on you.

concepts.title: Calculating Weight from Mass
concepts.explanation:
Because weight is the force of gravity on a mass, we can calculate it whenever we know the mass and how strong gravity is. The strength of gravity in a place is called the gravitational field strength, and we give it the symbol g. It tells you how many newtons of force pull on each kilogram of mass. On the surface of the Earth, g is about 10 newtons for every kilogram, which we write as g = 10 N/kg. (Scientists using very precise instruments measure it as 9.8 N/kg, and you will meet that more exact value later; for now we will use 10 N/kg because it makes the arithmetic clear.)

weight = mass x gravitational field strength, or in short symbols, W = m x g.

In this equation, weight (W) is in newtons, mass (m) is in kilograms, and gravitational field strength (g) is in newtons per kilogram. Let us work through several examples together. In each one, follow the four steps: write what you are given, write the formula, put the numbers in and calculate, and finally state the answer with its unit. Doing all four steps every time will keep your work clear and will earn full marks in any test.

Worked Example 1: The weight of a sack of rice on Earth.

Amina buys a sack of bariis (rice) with a mass of 25 kg. What is its weight on Earth, where g = 10 N/kg?

Given: mass m = 25 kg; gravitational field strength g = 10 N/kg.

Formula: W = m x g.

Calculate: W = 25 x 10 = 250.

concepts.title: The Solar System
concepts.explanation:
Lift your eyes from the ground now and look outward into space. Our home in the universe is called the Solar System. At its centre is the Sun, an enormous ball of extremely hot glowing gas. The Sun is a star, the same kind of object as the tiny points of light you see at night, but it looks huge and bright to us only because it is so much closer. The Sun's mass is so gigantic that its gravity reaches out across billions of kilometres and holds everything else in the Solar System in place.

Travelling around the Sun are eight planets. In order of distance from the Sun they are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. The four nearest the Sun, including our Earth, are rocky worlds. The four farthest out are giant balls of gas and ice, far larger than the Earth. Each planet moves around the Sun along a curved path called an orbit. The planets do not travel in perfect circles; their orbits are slightly stretched ovals, but they are close enough to circles that we can usually picture them as circles. Many planets also have moons, smaller bodies that orbit around them. Our Earth has one Moon, the bright companion that lights the savanna night and marks the months of the Hijri calendar.

How can scientists describe the Solar System when nobody has ever stood outside it to look? They use a model. A model is a way of representing something that we cannot see directly, so that we can understand it and make predictions. Long ago, some people believed the Earth stood still at the centre and everything went around it. Careful observation of how the planets move across the sky gave scientists evidence that contradicted that old idea, and supported a better model, one with the Sun at the centre and the planets, including Earth, orbiting around it. This is a beautiful example of how science works: we form a hypothesis, we observe carefully, and we change our ideas when the evidence points a different way. Scientists also think the whole Solar System formed long ago from a giant spinning cloud of dust and gas in space called a nebula.
concepts.example: Did You Know? Light from the Sun takes about eight minutes to reach the Earth, travelling faster than anything else in the universe. So when you feel the warm morning sun on your face in Mogadishu or Kampala, that warmth actually left the Sun about eight minutes ago. You are always seeing the Sun a little bit in the past.

concepts.title: Movement in Space
concepts.explanation:
Why do the planets keep going round and round the Sun without ever stopping or flying away? The answer is a partnership between two things: the planet's forward motion and the Sun's gravity. Each planet is moving forward through space very fast. At the same time, the Sun's gravity is constantly pulling it inward. If there were no gravity, the planet would shoot off in a straight line into deep space. If the planet were not moving forward, gravity would pull it straight into the Sun. Because both happen together, the planet is bent into a curved path, an orbit, endlessly falling around the Sun without ever falling in. The Moon orbits the Earth in exactly the same way.

Space is a vacuum, which means it is almost completely empty; there are no particles of air between the planets. This matters a great deal. On Earth, a moving object is always slowed by air resistance, a force caused by the object having to push the air out of its way. A ball you throw slows down and falls; a car must keep its engine running just to keep moving against the air. But in the vacuum of space there is no air to push against, so there is no air resistance. Once a planet or a spacecraft is moving, nothing slows it down, and it can keep travelling for billions of years. This is why the planets have circled the Sun for such an unimaginably long time.
concepts.example: Closer to home, the Earth is not only orbiting the Sun; it is also spinning on its axis, an imaginary line running through the North and South Poles. The Earth turns all the way round once about every 24 hours. As it turns, the side of the Earth facing the Sun has daytime, while the side facing away is in the shadow of space and has night. It is not the Sun that rises and sets; it is the Earth that is turning beneath it. When you watch the Sun climb over the acacia trees at dawn near Garissa, you are really feeling the ground you stand on rotating towards the Sun. The Earth takes one full year, about 365 days, to complete a single orbit of the Sun, and this yearly journey, together with the tilt of the Earth's axis, is what gives many parts of the world their seasons.

concepts.title: The Tides
concepts.explanation:
If you live near the coast, or have visited the Indian Ocean shore at Kismaayo, Mombasa, Lamu or Dar es Salaam, you have seen the tides. Twice each day the sea climbs up the beach, covering the sand and rocks; this is high tide. And twice each day it slides back down, uncovering a wide stretch of wet sand and exposing the reef; this is low tide. This steady, twice-daily rise and fall of the whole ocean is one of the clearest signs of gravity acting on a giant scale, and coastal fishermen plan their entire working day around it.

What causes the tides? The main cause is the gravitational pull of the Moon. Even though the Moon is far away, its gravity reaches across space and gently pulls on the Earth, and especially on the water of the oceans, because water can flow and move easily. The Moon's pull draws the ocean water into a slight bulge on the side of the Earth nearest the Moon. As the Earth spins on its axis through the day, different coastlines are carried into and out of these bulges, so the water seems to rise and fall from the point of view of a person standing on the shore. The Sun's gravity adds to this effect as well, though because the Sun is so far away, its influence on the tides is smaller than the Moon's. The difference in water depth between a high tide and a low tide is called the tidal range.

Because the Moon controls the tides, and because the Moon is also what the Hijri calendar follows, the coastal people of East Africa have long connected the rhythm of the sea with the phases of the Moon. When the Sun and the Moon line up, near the new Moon and the full Moon, their pulls combine to give especially large tides called spring tides, with very high highs and very low lows. When the Sun and the Moon pull at right angles to each other, about a week later, their effects partly cancel and we get smaller tides called neap tides. A fisherman at Berbera who knows the phase of the Moon can therefore predict whether the tide will be large or small, and can plan when it is safe to bring a boat into the harbour and when the reef will be exposed for gathering shellfish.

Everything in this unit has been about pull and movement, and behind all of it sits one idea: energy. Energy is what must be transferred for anything at all to happen — for the sea to climb the beach, for a boat to lift on the water, for a fisherman's arms to haul in a net.

Energy is stored in several ways, and their names are worth learning. A moving object carries kinetic energy: the running child, the falling date, the incoming tide. An object that has been lifted carries gravitational potential energy, ready to be released the moment it is let go — the higher and heavier it is, the more it holds. A stretched rubber band or a bent bow holds elastic energy. Food, charcoal and a battery hold chemical energy. A hot pot holds thermal energy. Light, sound and electricity are all ways energy travels from one place to another.

Energy is never created and never destroyed; it only moves from one store to another. Hold a stone above the ground and it holds gravitational potential energy. Let go, and gravity transfers that store into kinetic energy as the stone speeds up. When it strikes the sand the movement stops, but the energy has not vanished — it has gone into a small thud of sound and a slight warming of the stone and the ground where they met.

That last step matters more than it looks. Every transfer spills some energy into the surroundings as heat, spread thinly through the air and the ground. It is still energy, but it is now shared out so widely that nothing can be done with it. Scientists say the energy has dissipated. It is why a bicycle left to itself always rolls to a stop, why every machine grows warm as it works, and why no engine ever returns all the energy it is fed.
concepts.example: Did You Know? The tides do not happen at exactly the same clock time each day. Because the Moon is also moving along its own orbit, high tide arrives a little later each day, roughly fifty minutes later than the day before. Experienced fishing families along the Indian Ocean coast carry this timing in their heads without ever needing a printed table.

explorations.title: Build a Rubber-Band Forcemeter
explorations.context: To build a simple forcemeter (a device that measures force) from a rubber band, and to use it to compare the weights of different household objects.
explorations.prompt: Before you begin, write down what you think: Will a heavier object stretch the rubber band more or less than a lighter object? Why? Predict, then test.
explorations.answer: Which object stretched the band the most? What does that tell you about its weight compared with the others? Put your objects in order from lightest to heaviest, using only your stretch measurements. The rubber band stores elastic energy when it is stretched. Where does that energy come from when you load the bag? Why was it important to check that the band returned to its zero mark between objects?

explorations.title: The Swinging Pendulum
explorations.context: To build a pendulum and investigate what affects how long it takes to swing back and forth, watching gravity and energy at work.
explorations.prompt: Predict: Will a longer string make the pendulum swing faster or slower? Will a heavier weight change the swing time? Write your predictions before testing.
explorations.answer: Did shortening the string make the pendulum swing more times or fewer times in 30 seconds? So did it swing faster or slower? Did making the bob heavier change the number of swings very much? What does this tell you about how gravity pulls on light and heavy objects? At the top of each swing the bob pauses for an instant. At that moment, what kind of energy does it have the most of? At the bottom of the swing, moving fastest, what kind of energy does it have the most of? The pendulum slowly swings less and less far and finally stops. Where has its energy gone? (Think about the word 'dissipated'.)

methods.title: Build a Rubber-Band Forcemeter
methods.example: To build a simple forcemeter (a device that measures force) from a rubber band, and to use it to compare the weights of different household objects.
steps: Hang the rubber band from the nail or hook so it dangles freely.
Attach the empty bag or cup to the bottom of the band.
Hold the ruler next to the band and record the position of the bottom of the empty bag. This is your starting mark (zero load).
Place one object in the bag. Wait for it to stop moving, then record the new position of the bottom of the bag.
Work out how far the band stretched by subtracting the starting mark from the new position.

methods.title: The Swinging Pendulum
methods.example: To build a pendulum and investigate what affects how long it takes to swing back and forth, watching gravity and energy at work.
steps: Tie the bob securely to one end of the string.
Tie or hold the other end so the bob hangs freely and can swing without hitting anything.
Pull the bob gently to one side (a small angle) and release it without pushing.
Count how many complete swings (over and back) happen in 30 seconds. Record it.
Repeat twice more and take the average, to make your result more reliable.

methods.title: Falling Objects and Air Resistance
methods.example: To observe how gravity pulls objects down and how air resistance can change the way things fall.
steps: Hold one flat sheet of paper in each hand at the same height. Drop both at once and watch. (They should fall similarly.)
Now crumple one sheet into a tight ball. Hold the flat sheet and the crumpled ball at the same height.
Drop both at the same moment and carefully watch which lands first.
Repeat two or three times so you are sure of what you see.
Try the same idea with the stone and the feather or leaf.

methods.title: Modelling the Solar System and Day/Night
methods.example: To build a simple model of the Sun, Earth and Moon, and to use it to show why we have day and night and how the Moon orbits the Earth.
steps: Darken the room and place the lamp on a table as the Sun.
Mark a spot on the ball to be your town, for example Mogadishu.
Hold the ball at arm's length so the lamp lights one side of it. Notice that only the half facing the lamp is lit; the other half is in shadow.
Slowly rotate the ball on the spot (spinning it on its axis) and watch your marked town move from the lit side (day) into the shadow side (night) and back again.
Now walk the ball slowly all the way around the lamp to show the Earth's yearly orbit.

workedExamples.title: 1: The weight of a sack of rice on Earth.
workedExamples.prompt: Amina buys a sack of bariis (rice) with a mass of 25 kg. What is its weight on Earth, where g = 10 N/kg?
workedExamples.solution:
Given: mass m = 25 kg; gravitational field strength g = 10 N/kg.

Formula: W = m x g.

Calculate: W = 25 x 10 = 250.

Answer: The weight of the sack is 250 N on Earth.

workedExamples.title: 2: Your own weight.
workedExamples.prompt: Hassan has a mass of 40 kg. Calculate his weight on Earth (g = 10 N/kg).
workedExamples.solution:
Given: m = 40 kg; g = 10 N/kg.

Formula: W = m x g.

Calculate: W = 40 x 10 = 400.

Answer: Hassan weighs 400 N on Earth.

workedExamples.title: 3: The same person on the Moon.
workedExamples.prompt: The Moon's gravitational field strength is only about 1.6 N/kg, roughly one sixth of Earth's. What would Hassan weigh on the Moon, and what is his mass there?
workedExamples.solution:
Given: m = 40 kg (mass does not change); g on the Moon = 1.6 N/kg.

Formula: W = m x g.

Calculate: W = 40 x 1.6 = 64.

Answer: On the Moon Hassan would weigh only 64 N, but his mass is still 40 kg.

workedExamples.title: 4: Working backwards to find mass.
workedExamples.prompt: A goat is weighed on Earth and its weight is found to be 300 N. What is its mass? (g = 10 N/kg.)
workedExamples.solution:
Given: W = 300 N; g = 10 N/kg; we must find m.

Formula: Start from W = m x g, then rearrange to m = W / g.

Calculate: m = 300 / 10 = 30.

Answer: The goat's mass is 30 kg.

workedExamples.title: 5: A camel's weight.
workedExamples.prompt: A young camel has a mass of 220 kg. What is its weight on Earth (g = 10 N/kg)?
workedExamples.solution:
Given: m = 220 kg; g = 10 N/kg.

Formula: W = m x g.

Calculate: W = 220 x 10 = 2200.

Answer: The camel weighs 2200 N on Earth.

workedExamples.title: 6: Comparing two planets.
workedExamples.prompt: A rover has a mass of 180 kg. Calculate its weight on Earth (g = 10 N/kg) and on Mars (g = 3.7 N/kg), and describe what you notice.
workedExamples.solution:
Given: m = 180 kg; g(Earth) = 10 N/kg; g(Mars) = 3.7 N/kg.

Formula: W = m x g.

Calculate on Earth: W = 180 x 10 = 1800 N.

Calculate on Mars: W = 180 x 3.7 = 666 N.

workedExamples.title: Gravity is best described as
workedExamples.prompt: Gravity is best described as: (a) a contact force, (b) a non-contact force of attraction, (c) a push, (d) a form of energy.
workedExamples.solution: (b) a non-contact force of attraction Gravity acts across a gap, with no touching, and always pulls objects together.

workedExamples.title: The unit of mass is
workedExamples.prompt: The unit of mass is: (a) newton, (b) joule, (c) kilogram, (d) watt.
workedExamples.solution: (c) kilogram Mass is the quantity of matter, measured in kilograms.

activities.title: Build a Rubber-Band Forcemeter
activities.materials: One thick rubber band (or a length of thin elastic).; A small cloth bag, a light plastic cup, or a small tin with a handle, to hold objects.; A ruler or a strip of paper marked in centimetres.; A nail, hook, or door handle to hang the band from.; Several small objects to weigh: a spoon, a stone, a handful of dates, a small potato, a bar of soap.
steps: Hang the rubber band from the nail or hook so it dangles freely.
Attach the empty bag or cup to the bottom of the band.
Hold the ruler next to the band and record the position of the bottom of the empty bag. This is your starting mark (zero load).
Place one object in the bag. Wait for it to stop moving, then record the new position of the bottom of the bag.
Work out how far the band stretched by subtracting the starting mark from the new position.
Safety: Pins and nails have sharp points — ask an adult to help, and store them safely afterwards.

activities.title: The Swinging Pendulum
activities.materials: A length of string or strong thread (about one metre).; A small heavy object to act as the bob: a metal nut, a small stone in a cloth, or a key.; A fixed point to hang from: a door frame, a nail, or a stick held over the edge of a table.; A clock, watch or phone that can count seconds.
steps: Tie the bob securely to one end of the string.
Tie or hold the other end so the bob hangs freely and can swing without hitting anything.
Pull the bob gently to one side (a small angle) and release it without pushing.
Count how many complete swings (over and back) happen in 30 seconds. Record it.
Repeat twice more and take the average, to make your result more reliable.
Safety: Pins and nails have sharp points — ask an adult to help, and store them safely afterwards.

activities.title: Falling Objects and Air Resistance
activities.materials: Two identical sheets of paper.; A small stone and a feather or a dry leaf.; A safe, clear place to drop things from the same height (standing height is enough).
steps: Hold one flat sheet of paper in each hand at the same height. Drop both at once and watch. (They should fall similarly.)
Now crumple one sheet into a tight ball. Hold the flat sheet and the crumpled ball at the same height.
Drop both at the same moment and carefully watch which lands first.
Repeat two or three times so you are sure of what you see.
Try the same idea with the stone and the feather or leaf.

activities.title: Modelling the Solar System and Day/Night
activities.materials: A torch, lamp, or candle to act as the Sun (with adult help if using a flame).; A ball or a round fruit such as an orange to act as the Earth.; A small pebble or a smaller fruit to act as the Moon.; A small sticker or a spot of ink to mark 'your town' on the Earth-ball.; A darkened room.
steps: Darken the room and place the lamp on a table as the Sun.
Mark a spot on the ball to be your town, for example Mogadishu.
Hold the ball at arm's length so the lamp lights one side of it. Notice that only the half facing the lamp is lit; the other half is in shadow.
Slowly rotate the ball on the spot (spinning it on its axis) and watch your marked town move from the lit side (day) into the shadow side (night) and back again.
Now walk the ball slowly all the way around the lamp to show the Earth's yearly orbit.

activities.title: Observe: Movement in Space
activities.materials: One thick rubber band (or a length of thin elastic).; A small cloth bag, a light plastic cup, or a small tin with a handle, to hold objects.; A ruler or a strip of paper marked in centimetres.; A nail, hook, or door handle to hang the band from.; Several small objects to weigh: a spoon, a stone, a handful of dates, a small potato, a bar of soap.
steps: Look for an example of movement in space around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.

rules.title: Mass in Kilograms, Weight in Newtons
rules.text: Mass is measured in kilograms (kg) and never changes with location. Weight is a force, measured in newtons (N), and changes when gravity changes. A common shortcut in everyday life is to say something 'weighs 25 kilograms'. In science this is not correct: 25 kilograms is a mass. The weight would be about 250 newtons on Earth.

rules.title: Energy Transfers and Wasted Heat
rules.text: Energy is never created or destroyed; it is only transferred from one store to another. In every real transfer, some energy is dissipated (spread out, usually as heat) and becomes wasted energy. Useful energy plus wasted energy always adds up to exactly the energy you started with.

An imaginary line through a planet about which it spins.

commonMistakes: Kilograms measure mass, not force. Weight is a force.
Saying mass changes on the Moon
Mass is the amount of matter, which does not change with location.
Thinking there is no gravity in space
Gravity fills space; it holds planets and moons in orbit.
Saying heavier things always fall faster
This is only true because of air resistance.
Saying energy is 'used up' and lost
Thinking the Sun moves round the Earth
It is the Earth that spins on its axis.

connections.text: This unit builds on your knowledge of matter, particles and states of matter, since mass is about the quantity of matter in an object.
Energy transfers appear again in electricity, in food chains and respiration in living things, and in the study of light and sound.
The formula W = m x g uses multiplication, division and rearranging, the same skills you practise in maths.
Tides, coasts, harbours and the Indian Ocean link directly to your geography of the East African coast.
The lunar calendar, the phases of the Moon, and reflecting on the order of creation connect this science to daily life and to gratitude.
On a clear night away from city lights, find the Moon and try to identify one bright planet. Note the Moon's shape and watch how it changes over a week.

realProblems.prompt: Amina's sack of maize has a mass of 45 kg. Calculate its weight on Earth (g = 10 N/kg). Show all four steps.
realProblems.answer: Given: m = 45 kg, g = 10 N/kg. Formula: W = m x g. Calculate: W = 45 x 10 = 450. Answer: 450 N.

realProblems.prompt: A camel has a mass of 400 kg. Calculate its weight on Earth. Then calculate its weight on the Moon, where g = 1.6 N/kg. Comment on what changed and what did not.
realProblems.answer: On Earth: W = 400 x 10 = 4000 N. On the Moon: W = 400 x 1.6 = 640 N. The weight changed (from 4000 N to 640 N) because the Moon's gravity is weaker, but the mass stayed 400 kg because the amount of matter did not change.

realProblems.prompt: A fisherman at Kismaayo notices the sea is very high at the new Moon. Explain why the tide is especially large at this time.
realProblems.answer: At new Moon, the Sun and the Moon are lined up on the same side (or opposite sides) of the Earth, so their gravitational pulls combine. This produces an especially large spring tide, with a very high high tide and a very low low tide.

realProblems.prompt: A family in Garissa uses a solar panel to charge a battery, which at night powers a light. Describe the energy transfers, from sunlight to the glowing bulb, naming each form of energy.
realProblems.answer: Sunlight (light energy) hits the solar panel and is transferred to electrical energy. The battery stores it as chemical energy. At night the battery transfers electrical energy to the bulb, which gives out light energy (and some wasted thermal energy).

realProblems.answer: Mass: rearrange W = m x g to m = W / g = 200 / 10 = 20 kg. By being lifted up, the container gains gravitational potential energy.

realProblems.prompt: A rover has a weight of 720 N on Earth. Without a calculator, work out its mass, then predict roughly its weight on Mars (g = 3.7 N/kg). Explain your reasoning.
realProblems.answer: Mass = W / g = 720 / 10 = 72 kg. On Mars, W = 72 x 3.7 = about 266 N. Reasoning: mass is unchanged at 72 kg; Mars's gravity (3.7 N/kg) is weaker than Earth's, so the weight is much less.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the difference between mass and weight. Give the unit of each.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Mass is the quantity of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg), and it never changes with location. Weight is the force of gravity acting on that mass, measured in newtons (N), and it changes if gravity changes.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: State the relationship (formula) that connects weight, mass and gravitational field strength.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Weight = mass x gravitational field strength, or W = m x g. Weight is in N, mass in kg, and g in N/kg.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why does your weight change on the Moon but your mass stay the same?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Your mass is the amount of matter you are made of, which does not change when you travel. Your weight depends on how strongly gravity pulls, and the Moon's gravity is weaker than Earth's, so you weigh less there while your mass stays the same.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name the force that holds the planets in their orbits around the Sun.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The force of gravity, coming from the Sun, holds the planets in their orbits.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain, using the idea of the Earth's axis, why we have day and night.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The Earth spins on its axis roughly once every 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has day; the side turned away is in shadow and has night. As the Earth turns, each place passes from day into night and back.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What causes the tides, and why are there very large tides at new Moon and full Moon?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon (with a smaller pull from the Sun) drawing the ocean water into bulges. At new Moon and full Moon the Sun and Moon line up, so their pulls combine to give especially large spring tides.

selfAssessment: I can describe gravity as a non-contact force of attraction that exists around every object that has mass, and explain that it acts towards the centre of a planet or star.
I can explain why my weight changes on the Moon and on other planets while my mass stays the same.
I can describe the Solar System: the Sun at the centre, the eight planets and their orbits, and how a scientific model helps us picture what we cannot see directly.
I can explain movement in space: why planets orbit the Sun, why the Earth spinning on its axis gives us day and night, and why there is no air resistance in the vacuum of space.
I can explain the tides as the daily rise and fall of the ocean caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon, and describe spring tides and neap tides.
I can identify the main forms of energy (kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic, chemical, thermal, light, sound and electrical) and give an everyday example of each.
I can describe energy transfers, using the idea that energy is stored, then transferred from one store to another, and that some energy is always dissipated (wasted).
I can apply the principle that energy is never created or destroyed, only transferred from one store to another.
